reading.rtitle: The Update That Says What You Decided
paras: Every closing update that Laura Mendel receives is, in her words, a list of decisions dressed up as a list of facts. The BPO sent two entries late. The tax file arrived on day four. What she actually wants to hear is what you did about it, and that, she says, lives almost entirely in the verbs. I decided to escalate it. I managed to close on time anyway. I avoided posting anything until the numbers were confirmed. Three sentences, three decisions, and every one of them tells her something about the person speaking.

She has noticed that these verbs come in two families, and that people who mix them up sound less sure of their own decisions. Some verbs are followed by to and a base verb: decide to, agree to, plan to, refuse to, manage to. They tend to look forward, toward an action. Others take the -ing form: avoid, consider, recommend, risk, keep, finish. I recommend reviewing the entries once more is a recommendation. I recommend to review sounds, to her ear, like a translation.

The most useful verb in a difficult update, she says, is the one people least like to use: refuse. I refused to post the adjustment without support is not a confession of being difficult. It is evidence of a thorough review, and directors trust it more than any promise. The second most useful is risk, because it puts a price on a choice: if we post it today, we risk reopening the period in March.

And the verb she hears least, and wishes she heard more, is a phrasal one. I kept putting off the conversation with the BPO, and then I decided to have it on Monday. It is honest, it shows a change, and it uses both families in one breath. Most people, she says, have a sentence like that about their English as well. They just have not considered saying it out loud yet.
reading.source: A composite portrait of a regional finance director, written for this lesson.

listenings.text: I lead a BPO team that processes entries for eleven companies, and every month somebody's entry is late. I get two kinds of message about it. The first kind tells me what went wrong. The second kind tells me what the client decided to do, and what they recommend I do next. I decided to post the accrual manually this month. I recommend sending the file by Tuesday next time. I would like to avoid reopening the period. Those messages get answered first, every time, because I do not need to guess anything. The decision is already made, and my job is only to agree to it, or to explain why I cannot.

For years I avoided speaking in the regional call. I would prepare everything, and then let my manager present it, because I was afraid of getting stuck in the middle of a sentence. I kept putting it off, every quarter, with a different excuse. Then one month my manager was on vacation, and I had to do it. I did not manage to say everything I had planned, and I made at least four mistakes. But nobody remembered the mistakes. They remembered that the numbers were finally explained by the person who built them. After that, I decided to volunteer every quarter. I still prepare too much. But I have stopped apologizing for my accent.
